data.text: Revision with thick skin is the hardest rhinoplasty category, so your instinct to research hard is right. A few things that actually separate revision specialists: first, revisions should be a large share of their practice. Primary and revision rhinoplasty are different sports. Second, for thick skin, ask to see their thick-skinned patients at 12 months or more, not 3-month photos. Swelling in thick skin takes 12 to 18 months to settle, and early photos hide the real tip definition. Third, ask how they handle tip support with rib cartilage specifically. Graft resorption and warping risk should be discussed openly, not waved away. Red flags: a surgeon who promises the simulation exactly, or steers you toward the tiny upturned nose you said you do not want. Bring your simulation to consults, but judge the surgeon on their revisions, not their renderings.

From a surgeon's perspective: thick skin + rib-cartilage revision is one of the hardest combinations in rhinoplasty, so vetting matters more than the country. Three things I would look for: (1) before-afters of their own revision patients with thick skin specifically — primary thin-skin results do not transfer; (2) ask how many rib revisions they do per year — it is a different skill set from primary cases; (3) be cautious with anyone who promises your exact simulation — morphing shows direction, not a guarantee, and thick skin always softens tip definition. The fact that the online consults have not convinced you is actually good judgment — trust it.
